Card record of early data pertaining to organization of the club (5 July 1928-21 May 1930)
Excerpt from The Peking Rotarian (the Bulletin of the Rotary Club of Peking), July 5, 1928: “We hear that ‘Doc’ Faxon has not been idle since his arrival in Harbin. He has already succeeded in organizing a Masonic Lodge up there, and the next thing we expect he will accomplish is the formation of a Rotary club. We have been confidentially informed that the Bulletin of the new club – when it is formed will be called the ‘Zakuska’.”
Cable from District Governor Yoneyama received on 29 April 1930 : “Harbin Rotary Club organized April 24, Application following. All delighted with Mulholland Gundaker.”
Cable from District Governor Yoneyama received on 21 May 1930 : “Harbin Rotary Club application charter fee sent directly solicit special tolerance for mistaken course awaiting charter from board.”

Reporting that Manchuria has become a province of China (15 April 1929). Excerpt from Letter from F. Jirkovsky, to Director Schulz, dated 6 March 1929 (received 15 April 1929) : “After the death of Tchan-so-lin, his young son (at present the ruler of Manchuria with residence in Mukden) to prevent continuation of the civil war, recognized the present Government of China residing in Nanking, and permitted Manchuria to become a province of China and had the flags of United China (white sun and blue field) erected all over the province. (...) I am very much interested in Rotary and should appreciate to receive some more detailed explanation about this movement.”
Application for membership with list of officers and directors, 25 April 1930
Roster lists of charter members, 25 April 1930
Constitution and By-Laws, 26 May 1930.

Special Representative's Report to District Governor Transmitting Club Application for Membership in RI. Special Representative T. Sahara (Mukden) To the Governor of the 70th district, Surugacho Nihonbashiku, Tokyo. 24 April 1930. “This club was instituted on 24 April 1930 by Tokusuke Sahara with 22 charter members. On the 20th February 1930, Teiji Amano a Rotarian of Mukden, sounded the possibility of organizing a Rotary Club at HArbin and after consulting with President Sahara of Mukden, communicated with Governor Yoneyama about it and Amano had since seen leading residents in Harbin and had decided to establish a Rotary Club. On the 5th April 1930 Governor Yoneyama appointed President Sahara of Mukden as Special Representative of Governor District No. 70. Charter members of Rotary Club of Harbin met at Hotel Modern at 7 pm of the 24th April in the presence of President Sahara and Rotarian Amano of Mukden and all the necessary formality had been carried out and the organization was duly effected.” T. Sahara, Mukden, 24 April 1930.
Reporting that it is generally understood that Harbin is the dividing line between South and North Manchuria (22 May 1930)
Letter from Perry and Potter to President informing about the responsibilities of a president and forwarding relevant literature, 6, 20 June 1930.
Letter from Perry to Secretary informing about the responsibilities of a secretary and forwarding relevant literature, 6 June 1930.
Letter from Potter to President, 6 June 1930, 5 September 1930 : suggesting some adjustments to classification
Monthly report of new members (July 1930)

Special Commissioner James W. Davidson, to RI, dated 5 August 1930 questions the advisability of having a club in Harbin organized by the Japanese and offers to go to Manchuria and look the situation over. He offers to talk to Yoneyama and the Japanese district governor and have them understand that a place can have several clubs (Japanese, Chinese, European, etc). He was formerly consul in Manchuria and consequently, knows well the situation there. He expressed his astonishment before the fact that a Japanese club was organized in the Chinese capital of Manchuria (Mukden), and that Harbin is considered as being part of South Manchuria. “To organize a Japanese club there is as wrong as it would be to have only a Chinese club in Tokyo, and is likely to do all kinds of harm. I fear we will be severely criticized for it.”- > suggests disagreements within Rotary International.

Letter from Perry to RI Executive Committee, 16 August 1930 : reporting fear in China that Rotary is contributing to the Japanese penetration in China by organizing clubs in China composed entirely of Japanese. Special Comm. Davidson offers to go to Manchuria and look the situation over.

Monthly report of new members and changes of address (August 1930)
Yoshio Gundsi : Classification changed from Foreign Affairs to Business Counselling.

Letter from Yoneyama to Perry, 23 September 1930, sending pictures taken during Harbin charter night on August 31 and September 1, 1930, to be inserted in the Rotarian, with the following captions: No.1 The Sino-Japanese Enlightening Society Office where the charter night was held. No.2 Kowazaki, President of the Host Club, delivering opening address. No.3 Picnic at the village of Gokuraku near the Sungari River. No.4 On the way to Harbin from the village.
Memo of official visit by District Governor, 18 October 1930. Same comments as for other clubs in Manchuria “Frequent changes of the members due to the fact that the city is of colonial character.”.

Report on Club Administration to the District Governor, 2 December 1930. Club organized in 1930, has 22 members. Type of city : Agricultural and Industrial Center of North Manchuria. Population : 450,000. Classification and Membership: “Resignations are comparatively frequent though almost every month new members are elected.” “20% of club members know English and read the Rotarian, the rest simply look at it. “The question of language is the dead rock of this club.” Difficulty of getting Chinese members: (1) Chinese are the majority of the city. Great difficulty is to make them understand Rotary (not from linguistic difficulty). Greater difficulty is to make them Rotarians. (2) Very few Japanese members (the majority of the members being Japanese) know English. So are Russians. Russian is widely spoken, though not a small numbers do not understand it. Hence all speeches and announcements are made always in English, Japanese, and Russian. Three times same things. Weaknesses: Lack of permanent residents of this city. Leading men are almost all branch heads of some great firms.

Letter from Russell V. Williams to Kowazaki, President of Harbin Club, 21 January 1931, acknowledges receipt of copy of the Harbin Rotarian, cannot read articles in languages other than English but finds articles in English interesting, giving an insight into the cosmopolitan nature of Harbin.
Copy of Harbin Rotarian (December 1930) (mostly Japanese), including an article titled “A few words about Harbin and the Harbin Rotary Club, by Rotarian M. Yagi (p.5)
Russian translations of RI pamphlets (19 October 1931-25 January 1932)
Monthly report of new members, changes of address and membership termination (February-March 1931)

Letter from Williams to Kowazaki, 21 March 1931, notices that the Harbin club was not represented at the Annual Convention in Chicago, and requests that it be represented in the next Convention in Vienna.
Monthly report of new members, changes of address and membership termination (May 1931)
Credential Certificate at RI 1931 Convention in Vienna, Austria, 30 April 1931. Membership: 21. Two delegates: T. Kawasaki, Y. Gundsi. On proxy: Y. Hoshino, Osaka, Japan.
Club secretary reports of his success in securing contacts with Rotarians in other countries who are philatelists, especially in Zagreb (10 February-11 March 1931).

Correspondence with E. Lenox Simpson, Simpson’s Agencies (newspaper correspondent for London papers, speaks 5 languages), a former member of the Harbin RC who desires to be reinstated as a member, 17 February 1932: he claimed he was an unofficial member of the club before it was even formally recognized by RI, he was the first non-Japanese member to be elected, but then could not attend because of rheumatisms. He had a private conversation with RI commissioner Davidson, then touring Manchuria, and they agreed that it was not normal that an international city like Harbin was dominated by Japanese, and that it should include more Chinese and Russians who are more numerous than Japanese in Harbin. Also mentions that Harbin is a Russian built town and Russian is the most widely spoken foreign language there, but Japanese is used in Rotary, which prevents many non-Japanese speaking prospective members from joining the club. NB The letter sounds like a delation letter (the writer seems angry to have been excluded from the club), he denounces that the club acts contrarily to many RI practices (no nicknames, no songs, few entertainment, more like public function, no charities)

RI prefers not to interfere with local (Japanese) matters, 21-25 March 1932 : “in view of the generally disturbed conditions in Manchuria at the present time, we fell that we have got to be very careful about any correspondence we have with the Rotary Club of Harbin lest some unfortunate misunderstanding might arise out of such correspondence.”

Letter from James W. Davidson to RI, April 1932 (between 18-29 April) (Confidential outside of staff), characterizes Simpson as a nuisance (being alcoholic).
Simpson was the brother of Bertram Lenox Simpson (1877-1930) (who took control of the Maritime customs in Tianjin on behalf of warlord Yan Xishan and was killed in 1930. E. Lenox-Simpson was a British newspaper man, editor of a Russian-language newspaper in Harbin, financed by the Soviet (although according to Davidson, he was not communist).

Club bulletin (The Harbin Rotarian) for March 1, 1932, no.8, which gives a list of the meetings of the club during the year. 2 first pages covered with advertisements. Most articles are in English, but also Russian. Report of the secretary includes a detailed list of meetings, with the number of presents, absentees (with their names), percentage of attendance, chairman, business and speech. Attendance records.
Club bulletin, June 1932, no.10 - English and Japanese copies.
Letter from Nicolas S. Baitelin to RO, 16 June 1932, Asking if there is any way in which RI can aid the flood victims of Harbin.
Credential Certificate for the 1932 Convention in Seattle, Washington. 28 members. Proxy : Yoso Namura, (Yokohama)

Letter from District Governor Takashi Isaka, 5 August 1932 : reports he failed to visit the clubs in Manchuria (Dairen, Harbin, Mukden, and Keijo), having important affairs in Tokyo, but promises to do so later this year.
Request from Rotary Club of Harbin for relief for flood sufferers, 5 September 1932 (photos attached).

Club bulletin (The Harbin Rotarian) for November 1, 1932, no.12. The feature story is about the floods in Harbin (illustrated with photos). Also termination of membership (Fujita, charter member, leaves Harbin), transferred to Dairen. Report of secretary. Attendance record.
RI to Tomizo Takata, 11 November 1932 : sends congratulations for issuing “the finest bulletin in the 70th district” as characterized by the Tokyo Rotary Club bulletin.
Pamphlets in Russian
Letter from Williams to Takata, 9 February 1933 : worry about having received no news from the club for several months, and enquiring how things are going.
Reply March 16 1933 (replying business as usual)
Correspondence between RI, Rotary Club of Harbin, and Consul of Japan in Chicago, March-April 1933, sending mutual greetings.
Credential Certificate to 1933 Convention in Boston, 30 April 1933. Membership : 33. 2 delegates: Tomizo Takata, Tadao Kawasumi. Proxy : D.R. Young (Tokyo).

The Harbin Rotarian, August 1932, No.11.

Letter from Harbin Secretary (RAS Waters) to RI Secretary, “July 1st 1933 Semi-Annual Report”, 14 September 1933 : enclosing semi-annual report, demand draft of U.S.$81.97 and copy of membership list as at 1st July 1933.
Letter from Russell Williams to Tomiza Takata, President of Harbin Rotary Club, 18 October 1933 : expressing pleasure to receive the visit of Rotarian Adolphe E. Hassek of Harbin.

Harbin Rotary Club Monthly Bulletin, 31 October 1933, No.13 (typewritten) : attendance report, Minsky’s speech about anti-bandistry law, Rotarian’s adoption of nicknames but lack of “vocal talent” for singing.
Letter from R.A.S. Waters to RI Secretariat, 7 November 1933: informing RI that he was being transferred to Shanghai and succeeded by Y. Gundsi as Secretary.
Letter from Y. Gundsi to Williams (received 26 December 1933), enclosing Manchukuo flag and propaganda literature.

Harbin Rotary Club Monthly Bulletin, 31 March 1934, No.18 (typewritten) : attendance report, indication that no meeting was held on March 1 because of the Manchoukuo national holiday, report by president “Tiger” Kanai concering the conference of the three Manchurian clubs in February 1934, review of the March 1934 Enthronement Ceremonies in Hsinking (Capital of Manchukuo) by Rotarian “Plum” Li Shao-Keng.
